notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Build tools for the agent's workflow, not as a mirror of your existing API — Writing effective tools for agents (Anthropic)

  • Tool definitions as a contract the model selects against — Anthropic API: tool use

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Tool design principles — granularity, naming and error messages as the three levers.

  • Tool Schemas — how a schema is written and what the model sees.

What this note adds: the decision those levers imply — whether to expose your existing API surface or design a task-level one on top. The principles note says "favour consolidated tools"; this is what that costs, how to pick the boundary, and the step-count arithmetic that settles it.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The fork? Mirror your CRUD API, or design tools around the agent's task.
Why CRUD is expensive? Each primitive is a step; a task becomes five calls instead of one.
The cost of task-level tools? A layer to build and version, separate from the API it wraps.
What error messages must do? Tell the model what was wrong and what a valid call looks like.
The signal you got it wrong? The model chains three tools to do one obvious thing.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I design tools around what the agent is trying to accomplish, not around the API I happen to have. Exposing CRUD primitives looks free because the endpoints exist, but every primitive becomes a step, and steps are where cost and unreliability compound — a task that should be one call becomes five, each with its own chance of going wrong. The cost of task-level tools is a real layer to build and version. The tell that you've got the boundary wrong is watching the model chain three calls to do something a user would describe in one sentence.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Mirror the API (thin CRUD) Prototype, or the agent's tasks genuinely are single operations. Steps multiply; the model must know your data model to compose them. Tool names match endpoint names.
Task-level tools The agent's work maps to recognisable tasks a user would name. A layer to build, version and keep in sync with the API beneath. Tools read like verbs from the brief: issue_refund, find_similar_tickets.
Consolidated multi-purpose tool Many near-identical operations differing only by parameter. A large parameter space the model must navigate; harder to validate. Twelve endpoints that differ only by resource type.
Generic escape hatch (run_query, call_api) Never, in production, for anything that writes. No contract to validate against; authority silently moves to the model. "It needs flexibility" with no bounded set of operations.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Thin CRUD No new layer — the agent talks to existing endpoints. More steps per task, so cost grows and p^N gets a bigger exponent. Failures are API errors the model must interpret without context.
Task-level A tool layer that composes API calls behind one operation. Fewer steps per task; each call does more. Tool-level metrics become meaningful — success rate per task, not per endpoint.
Consolidated One tool, a larger schema, and argument validation that carries the load. Fewer definitions in the prompt, which helps selection at scale. Argument errors become the dominant failure; the schema is the thing to tune.
Escape hatch Nothing — and no boundary either. Cheap to build, unbounded to operate. Nothing to enforce; injection reaches the action directly.

The redraw test: task-level tools add a composition layer between the loop and your services. If the diagram has the loop calling your REST endpoints directly, you chose the thin option — which may be right for a prototype and is worth saying out loud either way.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The step arithmetic that decides it. Suppose issuing a refund needs: look up the order, check eligibility, create the refund, update the ticket, notify the customer. As CRUD primitives that's five model-mediated steps. At a per-step success rate of 0.97, end-to-end is 0.97^5 ≈ 0.86. Collapsed into one issue_refund tool whose internals are ordinary code, the model makes one decision — and the arithmetic becomes 0.97, with the four composed operations running at whatever reliability your normal service code has.

The cost side. Each of those five steps also re-bills the accumulated context. Collapsing five steps into one removes four calls and their share of the steps² growth, which is why tool granularity is usually a bigger cost lever than model routing on agents that do real work.

The boundary test. Draw the tool boundary where a user would describe a unit of work. "Issue a refund" is a task; "update the refunds table" is an implementation detail. If a tool's name needs a conjunction to explain — "creates a refund and also updates the ticket" — that's fine, that's composition. If it needs a disjunction — "creates or updates or deletes depending on the mode parameter" — it's probably three tools wearing one name.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The error-message requirement at the end is not a detail. A tool that returns {"error": "invalid request"} converts a recoverable step into a loop, because the model has nothing to correct. The contract is: say what was wrong, and say what a valid call looks like.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "It takes eleven steps to do what a support rep does in one click, and it gets the order wrong sometimes."

Root cause. The tool layer had been generated from the existing OpenAPI spec, so the agent had forty thin tools mirroring REST endpoints. Issuing a refund required composing six of them in the right sequence, which meant the model had to know the internal data model — that a refund references a payment intent, which references an order — and get the ordering right every time. It usually did. "Usually" across six steps is where the failures came from, and each one looked like a different bug.

Fix. Three task-level tools replaced the forty, with the sequencing moved into ordinary service code where it could be tested. Step count per task dropped from eleven to three, and the class of ordering bugs disappeared entirely — not because the model got better at sequencing, but because sequencing stopped being its job.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

You already have an API. Why not just expose it?

Because an API is designed for a programmer who has read the docs and holds the data model in their head. A tool definition is read by a model that has a few hundred tokens of description and must choose correctly under ambiguity. Those are different consumers with different needs.

The practical difference is composition. A programmer composing five calls is normal; a model composing five calls is five chances to pick wrong, in an order it has to infer. Moving the composition into code is what makes the difference, and the API underneath doesn't change at all.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Task-level tools are a layer you maintain. When is the thin version genuinely better?

When the agent's job really is single operations — a data-retrieval agent where every task is one query, or an internal tool where the surface is small and stable. Building a composition layer over three endpoints is ceremony.

The other case is early exploration. If I don't yet know which tasks matter, exposing primitives lets the agent show me which sequences it actually performs — and those sequences are the specification for the task-level tools I'll write next. That's a deliberate temporary state, though, and it should come with the expectation that the traces get read.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

At fifty task-level tools, does this advice still hold?

The granularity advice holds but a new problem arrives: selection. Fifty definitions is a lot of prompt, and the model's accuracy at choosing degrades as near-duplicates accumulate — two tools whose descriptions overlap will be confused regardless of how well each is designed individually.

So at that size I'd namespace by domain and give each agent a subset rather than the catalogue, and for genuinely large surfaces retrieve tool definitions per request instead of listing them all. What I'd resist is consolidating tools just to reduce the count, because that trades a selection problem for an argument-space problem — the model now has to navigate a large parameter surface instead of a large tool list, and argument errors are harder to diagnose than selection errors.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the tool layer for a platform where service teams expose capabilities to agents.

I'd make the unit of publication a task, not an endpoint, and refuse to auto-generate tools from OpenAPI specs — because the generated surface is precisely the wrong granularity and it arrives at volume. A team publishes a tool with a name, a typed schema, a description written for a model, actionable error strings, and its direction and autonomy rung.

The platform would enforce what teams can't be relied on to do consistently: schema validation, error-string linting against a checklist, and a review step that asks whether a user would name this as one task. That last one can't be automated, but it can be a required field — "what user-facing task does this serve?" — and an empty or circular answer is a good signal the granularity is wrong.

What I'd measure is steps-per-task per agent over time. If it's rising as the catalogue grows, tools are being published at primitive granularity and the composition burden is landing back on the models.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Generate tools from the OpenAPI spec — it's the fastest way to full coverage."

✅ Reality: It gives you the wrong granularity at scale and instantly. The spec describes your resources; the agent needs your tasks. Coverage of endpoints isn't coverage of capability, and the composition burden lands on the least reliable component.

❌ Trap: "More tools means more capability."

✅ Reality: Past a point it means worse selection. Near-duplicate descriptions confuse the model, and each definition costs prompt tokens on every call. Capability comes from the right tools being unambiguous, not from the catalogue being large.

❌ Trap: "Error messages are for humans reading logs."

✅ Reality: The model is the first consumer of a tool error and it's the one that has to recover. An error that says what was wrong and what a valid call looks like turns a failed step into a corrected one; {"error": "bad request"} turns it into a retry loop that burns the step budget.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Tool design principles — the three levers this decision applies.

  • Tool error handling — the error contract, in full.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §4 Read tools vs write tools — direction is assigned per tool once the tools exist.

  • §4 Tool selection at scale — granularity determines how fast the catalogue grows.

  • §8 Compounding error — every step collapsed into a tool removes a term from p^N.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — issue_refund versus six CRUD calls is this decision.

  • §14 Data / SQL analyst agent — the escape-hatch row is why run_query is the wrong shape.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Constrained decoding — guaranteeing schema conformance at sampling time — OpenAI: structured outputs

  • Tool input schemas as the contract the model is held to — Anthropic API: tool use

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Structured Output & Constrained Decoding — how a schema is compiled into a decoding constraint.

  • Tool Schemas — what the schema expresses and what the model sees.

What this note adds: the boundary's two jobs, which get conflated. Constrained decoding guarantees shape; it says nothing about whether the values are permitted. The sibling note Where authority to act lives places the boundary; this decides what runs inside it, and in what order.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The two jobs? Shape (is it well-formed) and semantics (are these values allowed).
What constrained decoding gives? Shape, guaranteed — no retry needed. Nothing about permission.
What it can't check? That amount: 50000 is a legitimate refund for this user.
Order of checks? Shape → semantic → authorisation → execute. Cheapest first.
The never-do? Execute a free-form string the model produced.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I use constrained decoding for shape wherever the provider supports it, because a guaranteed-valid JSON object removes a whole class of retry loop for free. But shape is only half the boundary's job — a perfectly well-formed call can still be asking to refund fifty thousand pounds to the wrong account. So after shape I run semantic validation against business rules and then authorisation against the acting user's scope, in that order because each is more expensive than the last. The thing I never do is execute a string the model produced; if a tool takes free-form input, the boundary has nothing to enforce.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Constrained decoding The provider supports it and the schema is expressible. Provider lock-in on the feature; complex schemas can degrade quality. Structured extraction or a tool with a fixed argument shape.
Post-hoc validation + retry No constrained decoding available, or the schema is dynamic. A retry loop on malformed output — tokens and latency per failure. Older models, or a schema assembled at runtime.
Both (the production answer) Anything with real effects. Slightly more code; nothing meaningful in latency. Constrained shape, then your own semantic and scope checks.
Trust the model Never, once the call has an effect. Everything. Injected content reaches the action unfiltered. "We instruct it in the prompt to stay within bounds."

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Constrained decoding Schema compiled at the model call, not checked after. Removes malformed-output retries entirely — a real token saving. Schema changes become model-call changes; watch for quality effects.
Post-hoc + retry A validator plus a bounded retry path back to the model. Pays tokens per malformed attempt; capped by the retry limit. Malformed rate is a live metric and a model-drift signal.
Both Validator layers: shape, then semantics, then scope, before execute. Negligible per call; saves the downstream cost of a wrong action. Rejection reason becomes the useful field — shape vs semantic vs scope.
Trust No boundary at all. Cheapest until the incident. Nothing to monitor, which is how you find out late.

The redraw test: "both" puts a validation stage between the loop and the effect, with three named checks inside it. If your picture has one arrow labelled "call tool", the semantic and scope checks don't exist yet.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

What each layer actually catches. Shape errors are common early and vanish with constrained decoding. Semantic errors — a well-formed call with values that violate a business rule — persist regardless of model quality, because the model doesn't know your rules unless you told it, and even then it isn't bound by them. Scope errors are rarest and most expensive: a valid operation the caller wasn't entitled to perform. The layers are ordered by cost, so run them cheapest-first and reject early.

Why order matters for cost. Shape validation is microseconds against a compiled schema. Semantic validation may hit a database. Authorisation may hit an identity service. Running them in that order means a malformed call never reaches the identity service, which matters when the malformed rate spikes — and a spike is exactly what an injection attempt looks like.

The measurement worth keeping. Log the rejection reason, not just the rejection. A rising share of semantic rejections usually means prompt drift or a rule change nobody propagated; a rising share of scope rejections is more interesting, because it means something is asking for actions outside its entitlement — which is either a bug or an attack, and both deserve a look at the payloads.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

Note the asymmetry between the two rejection paths. A shape or semantic failure goes back to the model with an actionable message, because the model can fix it. A scope failure does not — it's denied and audited, because telling the model how to pass an authorisation check is telling an attacker.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The schema validation passed and it still did the wrong thing."

Root cause. The team had adopted structured outputs and treated schema conformance as the safety boundary — if the JSON matched, the call executed. An agent handling account changes emitted a perfectly valid update_plan call with a target account id taken from a document in its context rather than from the authenticated session. Every field was the right type, the enum value was legal, and the call was for a different customer. Nothing in shape validation could have caught it, because the shape was correct.

Fix. An authorisation check between validation and execution, resolving the acting user from the session rather than from arguments, and rejecting any call whose target the caller couldn't access. The general lesson is that constrained decoding solves a parsing problem and is frequently mistaken for solving a security one.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

If constrained decoding guarantees the schema, what's left to validate?

Everything about meaning. A schema says amount is a number and currency is one of three strings. It can't say that this user's refund limit is £200, that the order is already refunded, or that the caller isn't entitled to touch this account at all. Those are business rules and entitlements, and they live in your code.

The distinction I'd make explicit is that shape validation protects your parser and semantic validation protects your domain. They're both necessary and they fail differently — and conflating them is how a well-formed wrong action ships.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Constrained decoding can degrade output quality on complex schemas. Is it always worth it?

Not always, and the trade is real — heavily constrained decoding on a deeply nested schema can push the model toward filling required fields with plausible nonsense rather than declining. Where I see that, the fix is usually to simplify the schema rather than abandon the constraint: fewer required fields, optionals where the model might genuinely not know, and an explicit "unknown" value so it has a legal way to express uncertainty.

If the schema genuinely can't be simplified, post-hoc validation with a retry is a reasonable fallback, and the cost is bounded by the retry cap. What I wouldn't do is skip shape checking entirely because constrained decoding was awkward.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

At high volume, the semantic checks hit the database on every call. What gives?

The ordering already helps, since malformed calls never reach that layer. Beyond that I'd split semantic validation into what's cacheable and what isn't — a user's refund limit or entitlement set changes rarely and can be resolved once per run rather than per call, while "is this order already refunded" is inherently live and has to be checked at execution time anyway.

That points at the deeper answer: some semantic checks are better enforced by the downstream service than by the boundary, because the service owns the invariant and can enforce it transactionally. The boundary's job is to reject the obviously wrong cheaply and pass a well-formed, authorised call to a service that will still refuse an illegal state change. Duplicating every business rule at the boundary creates two places for the rule to live and one of them to be stale.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design validation for a platform where many teams' tools share one boundary.

I'd make the three layers a platform pipeline with team-supplied policies. Shape comes from the declared schema, which the platform compiles for constrained decoding automatically — teams never hand-write that. Semantics is a team-supplied predicate over the validated arguments. Authorisation is platform-owned entirely, because entitlement is a cross-cutting concern and teams implementing it individually is how you get inconsistency.

The critical design choice is that teams cannot skip a layer. A tool registered without a semantic predicate gets a default that rejects nothing — which is fine and explicit — but the authorisation layer always runs and cannot be opted out of, because that's the one whose absence is a security bug rather than a quality one.

What I'd expose is the rejection reason taxonomy, consistently across teams, so the platform can answer "which tools are being asked to do things their callers aren't entitled to" without each team instrumenting it separately.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We use structured outputs, so tool calls are validated."

✅ Reality: Structured outputs guarantee the call parses. They say nothing about whether the values are permitted, the target is in scope, or the operation is legal in the current state. Shape is the cheapest check, not the meaningful one.

❌ Trap: "Tell the model the rules in the prompt and it will respect them."

✅ Reality: Prompt instructions compete with instructions arriving through tool results and retrieved content, and the model isn't bound by either. Rules that matter are code on the other side of the boundary.

❌ Trap: "Send the authorisation failure back to the model so it can correct the call."

✅ Reality: Shape and semantic failures are correctable and should be returned with actionable messages. An authorisation failure is not a correction opportunity — explaining how to pass the check is a hint to whatever produced the call, which may not be your user.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Structured Output & Constrained Decoding — the shape layer's mechanism.

  • permissions and least privilege — what the authorisation layer enforces.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §2 Where authority to act lives — this note is what runs at that boundary.

  • §4 Tools are an API contract — an untyped tool makes this decision unenforceable.

  • §11 Indirect prompt injection — the scope layer is what an injected instruction fails against.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — the account-id failure story is that design's core risk.

  • §14 Data / SQL analyst agent — a read-only role is the authorisation layer expressed as a grant.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The idempotency-key contract, and why GET/DELETE need no key while POST does — Stripe API: idempotent requests

  • Why idempotency is an API design property rather than a retry trick — Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (Stripe)

  • Guardrails and the human-intervention trigger on consequential actions — A practical guide to building agents (OpenAI, PDF)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Tool design principles — granularity, naming and error messages as the three levers of a good tool.

  • Tool error handling — idempotency in the retry sense: don't retry a non-idempotent write.

  • permissions and least privilege — scoped credentials and the confused deputy.

What this note adds: direction as a classification axis for the whole catalogue — the default-deny posture for writes and what a tool inherits the moment it mutates state. Where authority to act lives decides where the boundary sits; this decides what a tool gets once it's on the write side.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The posture? Reads default-allow, writes default-deny. Direction decides, not the tool's name.
What every write tool inherits? An idempotency key, a user-scoped credential, and its own gate.
Why an idempotency key at all? A retried or duplicated call must not double the effect.
The number to quote? Share of tool calls that mutate state — usually small, and it's the whole risk.
The hidden write? A "read" that has a side effect: search that logs, GET that mutates a counter.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I classify every tool by direction first, because direction decides the defaults. Reads are default-allow — scoped to the user, but the agent calls them freely. Writes are default-deny: each one needs an idempotency key, a credential scoped to the acting user, and its own gate, and it doesn't ship until it has all three. The reason direction is the axis rather than sensitivity is that it's checkable in code — I can enumerate which tools mutate state and audit that set, whereas "is this tool dangerous" is a judgement someone forgets to make when they add the fourteenth tool.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Default-allow everywhere Prototypes, read-only analysis, no real side effects. The first write tool added inherits the wrong default, silently. Every tool is a retrieval; nothing in the catalogue mutates.
Default-deny everywhere Regulated domains, or an agent acting on many tenants' data. Reads pay gate latency for no risk reduction; the agent feels sluggish and over-supervised. Compliance owns the tool list, or every action is auditable by law.
Split by direction (the default) Almost always — a read-heavy catalogue with a few mutations. Two policy paths, and you must police the "read" that quietly writes. The catalogue is mostly get_* / search_* with a handful of create_*.
Split by blast radius, not direction A write surface where some mutations are trivial and others are not. Judgement per tool, which decays as the catalogue grows and people rush. Writes range from "set a preference" to "issue a refund".

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Default-allow No gate, no key store, no scoping layer. Fastest and cheapest per call. Nothing to monitor at the boundary; you find out from users.
Default-deny Every call passes policy; a key store and audit log for all of it. Gate latency on every call, including the 90% that are reads. One dashboard, but a noisy one — most rejections are irrelevant.
Split by direction Read path straight through with scoping; write path adds idempotency keys, a gate, and an audit record. p95 depends on the read/write mix; writes dominate latency, reads dominate token spend. Two signals: read egress volume, and write rejection/approval rate.
Split by blast radius A per-tool policy table with thresholds, rather than a two-lane split. Same as direction plus the cost of maintaining the table. Someone owns the table. A new tool without a rung is a release blocker.

The redraw test: choosing split-by-direction puts an idempotency key store and a gate on the write lane of the diagram, and leaves the read lane a straight line. If your picture has one undifferentiated arrow from loop to tools, you've chosen default-allow whether or not you said so.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The share that matters. Count the catalogue by direction:

write_share = mutating_tools / total_tools

In most agents this lands low — a dozen retrieval tools, two or three mutations — and that asymmetry is the argument for the split: expensive controls on a small minority of the surface, which is why default-deny on writes is affordable and default-deny on everything isn't.

Why the key isn't optional on that lane. Stripe's contract is the reference: all POST requests take an Idempotency-Key; GET and DELETE need none, being idempotent by definition. The server stores the status and body of the first request per key — including failures — and replays it on retry. For an agent, the key is what makes a retried call safe, and retries aren't hypothetical: a timeout mid-write is exactly when the loop tries again.

Key lifetime, which people get wrong. Stripe prunes keys after roughly 24 hours, and a reused key past that generates a new request. So the key must be derived from the run and step, never generated fresh on retry — otherwise the second attempt looks like a new request and duplicates the effect. That's the detail that fails in production.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The questions, in order:

  1. Does calling it change state anywhere? Including outside your system — an email sent, a webhook fired, a third-party record created. This is the only question that assigns the lane.

  2. Is it secretly a write? A search that writes an audit row, a GET that decrements a quota, a "preview" that reserves inventory — these inherit read defaults and shouldn't.

  3. Can the effect be undone cheaply? Reversible writes get a key and an audit record; irreversible ones get a gate too — the §1 autonomy decision applied per tool.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "A customer got the same 'we've received your request' email four times during a test run."

Root cause. The catalogue had grown to eleven tools, ten of them reads, and the eleventh — send_notification — was added alongside with the same defaults and no idempotency key, because nothing in the tool interface asked for one. During an eval run against a staging config still pointing at the live mail provider, a transient timeout made the send look failed, the generic retry fired, and each attempt delivered. The read/write distinction had never been made, so a write inherited a posture designed for retrieval.

Fix. Direction became a required field on the tool registration, writes got a key derived from run id plus step index, and the eval environment lost its credentials for external effects entirely. The lesson: this wasn't a retry bug — retries were correct. A write shipped with read defaults, which happens whenever direction isn't a field someone must fill in.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why split on direction rather than on how dangerous the tool is?

Because direction is mechanically checkable and danger is a judgement. I can enumerate which tools mutate state and assert on that set in CI; I can't assert that someone assessed risk correctly under deadline. The controls I want — keys, scoping, gating — are exactly the ones mutations need, so the cheap axis and the useful axis coincide.

Danger still matters, but within the write lane: it decides whether a write also needs a gate on top of its key. Direction picks the lane; blast radius picks the treatment inside it.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Reads are default-allow. Isn't an over-broad read the bigger risk, given exfiltration?

It's a real risk needing a different control. Reads don't need gates — a human approving a search is pointless — they need scoping: the credential is the end user's, not the agent's service account, so the agent reads only what the user could. That kills the confused-deputy case without adding latency to every call.

The exfiltration concern is about combining a broad read with an outbound path, so I'd treat it at egress: allowlist where the agent can send data, and count any tool that can transmit as a write whatever it's called. A tool that POSTs to an arbitrary URL is a write even if it feels like a fetch.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

At fifty tools across several teams, how do you keep the classification honest?

I'd make direction a required registration field and generate enforcement from it — a tool declared a write gets its key parameter and gate wired automatically, so declaring correctly is the easiest path. The failure at scale isn't malice; it's a team registering a mutation as a read because that path had less boilerplate.

So I'd add a CI check diffing declared direction against observed behaviour — a tool declared read that causes a non-GET call downstream fails the build. Imperfect, but it catches the wrapper that quietly POSTs. The other scaling problem is key derivation: with parallel tool calls, run-id alone isn't unique, so the key needs the step and call index or concurrent writes collide.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the write path for an agent operating across multiple tenants.

The write lane becomes a service rather than a library, because key uniqueness, audit completeness and credential scoping all have to hold across processes. A write goes through one path: resolve identity by token exchange, derive the key from run and step, check tenant-and-tool policy, execute, record the outcome against the key before returning.

Storing the result against the key is what makes retries safe rather than merely discouraged — the Stripe contract applied internally. A replay returns the stored result, including a stored failure. Key retention then caps how long a run can pause mid-write and still resume safely, which matters because approval gates make multi-day pauses normal.

Per-tenant isolation runs through all of it: separate credentials, audit streams and policy. I'd watch write rejection rate per tenant — a spike is usually a prompt regression or an injection attempt, and both want someone reading the rejected payloads.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "The tool is named get_*, so it's a read."

✅ Reality: Direction is about effects, not names. A get_quote that reserves inventory, a search that writes an audit row, a preview that charges — all writes. Verify what happens downstream rather than trusting the signature.

❌ Trap: "We handle duplicates with retry logic — we don't retry writes."

✅ Reality: The agent isn't the only source of duplication. A model can emit the same call twice in one turn, a run can resume from a checkpoint that already executed, a user can retry the request. Keys cover all three; a no-retry rule covers one.

❌ Trap: "Approval gates make idempotency keys unnecessary — a human checks each write."

✅ Reality: Different problems. A gate stops the wrong action; a key stops the right action happening twice. A gated refund approved once and delivered twice by a resume is still a duplicate, and the approver will reasonably say they clicked once.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Tool design principles — granularity and naming, which this note assumes are already right.

  • Tool error handling — idempotency in the retry sense; this note makes it a property of the lane.

  • permissions and least privilege — the scoping half of the read lane.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §2 Where authority to act lives — this note's lanes are what that boundary enforces.

  • §1 Autonomy level — the rung is applied per write tool, which is why writes need their own gate.

  • §7 Partial completion & orphaned side effects — idempotency keys are half of the exactly-once story; the outbox is the other half.

  • §4 Parallel tool calls — concurrent writes to shared state are where key derivation gets hard.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — refunds and account changes are the canonical write lane.

  • §14 Data / SQL analyst agent — a read-only role is this decision expressed as a database grant.

  • §14 Internal agent platform — the Tier 4 write service is the platform form of this split.

notes.title: What to do when the catalogue outgrows the prompt
notes.category: Agentic System Design (§4 Tool Layer Design)

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Tool-definition tokens are prompt tokens — the cost of listing everything — Anthropic API: tool use

  • Retrieving tool definitions instead of listing them, as a scaling pattern — Writing effective tools for agents (Anthropic)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Tool selection at scale — tool retrieval, namespacing and per-agent toolsets.

What this note adds: the order to apply them in. The concept note lists the techniques; the decision is that per-agent subsets come first and tool retrieval last, because the cheapest fix is usually giving each agent fewer tools rather than building a retrieval layer.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The order to try? Prune duplicates → per-agent subsets → namespacing → retrieval.
Why retrieval last? It's a system to build; the first three are configuration.
The real failure at scale? Near-duplicate descriptions, not catalogue size.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

When a catalogue gets large the instinct is to build tool retrieval, and that's usually the fourth thing to try rather than the first. Selection degrades mostly because of near-duplicates — two tools whose descriptions overlap will be confused regardless of how many there are — so I prune and disambiguate first. Then I give each agent only the tools its job needs, which is configuration rather than engineering. Namespacing helps the model tell families apart. Retrieval is genuinely necessary past a few hundred tools, and it adds a failure mode: the right tool can now be absent from the prompt entirely.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Prune and disambiguate Always first. Two tools do nearly the same thing. An afternoon reading descriptions. The model picks the wrong one of a similar pair.
Per-agent toolsets Different agents or tasks need different subsets. A mapping to maintain as the catalogue grows. One agent, forty tools, and it uses six.
Namespacing Families of tools across domains: billing.*, tickets.*. Renaming, and a convention teams must follow. Names collide across teams: two search tools.
Tool retrieval Hundreds of tools and the subsets genuinely vary per request. A retrieval system, and the right tool can now be missing. You can't enumerate the needed subset before the request arrives.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Prune Fewer definitions; no new components. Removes prompt tokens on every call. Selection accuracy improves without anything to operate.
Per-agent subsets A tool-to-agent mapping in config. Smallest prompt per agent; biggest cheap win. A new tool needs an owner decision: which agents get it.
Namespacing Naming convention plus a registry that enforces it. Marginal token cost; better disambiguation. Rename migrations; old names need aliasing for a while.
Retrieval A tool index and a retrieval step before the model call. Retrieval latency per call, against saved prompt tokens. Recall becomes a metric — a missing tool is now a silent failure.

The redraw test: only retrieval adds a box. The first three change configuration and naming, which is why they're worth exhausting before building anything.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "It keeps calling search_docs when it should call search_tickets, and we've rewritten the prompt four times."

Root cause. Two teams had each shipped a search tool. One described itself as "search the knowledge base for relevant information"; the other as "search for relevant information in the support system". To a model choosing from a list, those are the same sentence with different nouns, and the agent picked whichever appeared first about as often as not. The catalogue was only twenty tools — the problem was never size, it was that two entries were not distinguishable from their descriptions.

Fix. Both were renamed into namespaces and their descriptions rewritten to lead with the distinguishing fact — what corpus each searches and when to prefer it — including an explicit "use this instead of X when…" line. Selection accuracy recovered without any retrieval layer. The general point is that the model is choosing from text, so the fix is nearly always in the text.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Tool selection at scale — the techniques this note orders.

  • Tool design principles — naming as a selection signal.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §4 Tool granularity — how fast the catalogue grows is set by that decision.

  • §6 Multi-agent topology — per-agent toolsets are sometimes the honest reason to split agents.

  • §5 Context budget — tool definitions are prompt tokens on every single call.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Internal agent platform — a shared registry across teams is where namespacing stops being optional.

  • §14 Support agent — a handful of well-named tools beats a catalogue every time.

notes.title: Which tool calls are safe to run in parallel
notes.category: Agentic System Design (§4 Tool Layer Design)

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Parallel tool use — the provider mechanism and how results return — Anthropic API: tool use

  • Idempotency keys, which is what makes a parallel retry safe — Stripe API: idempotent requests

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Parallel Tool Calling & Tool Batching — the mechanism and batching.

  • concurrency and parallelism — how concurrency works across an agent run.

What this note adds: the eligibility rule. Parallelism is the biggest latency lever available, and the decision is which calls qualify — which turns out to be the ordinary read/write concurrency question with a non-deterministic scheduler.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The eligibility rule? Reads parallelise freely; writes to the same resource never do.
Why it's the biggest latency lever? Wall-clock becomes the slowest call, not the sum.
The hidden hazard? Key derivation — run id alone isn't unique across parallel calls.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Parallel tool calls are the largest latency lever in an agent, because they turn a sum into a max. The eligibility rule is the ordinary one: reads parallelise freely, and writes to the same resource don't — the model has no concurrency model, so if I let it emit two writes to one record I've handed a race to a non-deterministic scheduler. In practice I allow parallel reads by default, serialise writes per resource, and make sure idempotency keys include the call index, because with parallel calls a run-and-step key is no longer unique.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Parallel reads, serial writes (default) Almost always. Write-heavy steps stay slow. A mix of retrieval and a few mutations.
Full parallel All calls are reads, or writes touch disjoint resources. You must prove disjointness; the model won't. Fan-out over independent items.
Fully serial Order matters semantically, or shared state has no locking. The latency sum — often the dominant cost in p95. Create-then-update sequences on one entity.
Parallel with per-resource locks Genuinely concurrent writes across many resources. Lock management, and deadlock as a new failure mode. High write volume across a partitioned space.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Parallel reads A fan-out/gather in the executor; results merged before the next step. Same tokens, much better wall-clock. Partial failure handling: does one dead call fail the step?
Full parallel No serialisation at all; disjointness asserted at registration. Best latency available. A wrong disjointness claim is a data race you'll find in production.
Serial Nothing — the simple path. Latency is the sum of every call. Easiest to reason about; the tail is your p95.
Per-resource locks A lock manager keyed by resource id. Lock wait time; contention under load. Deadlock detection and timeouts become yours.

The redraw test: parallelism puts a fan-out and a gather in the diagram, and the gather is where partial failure has to be decided. If there's no gather node, nobody has decided what one failed branch does.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Two of the three updates landed and the third silently didn't, and the agent reported success."

Root cause. The agent emitted three tool calls in one turn to update three fields on the same record, and the harness executed them in parallel because they were independent calls. They weren't independent writes — each did a read-modify-write of the whole record, so the last to complete overwrote the other two. The agent saw three success responses, because each call had genuinely succeeded; the losses happened at the datastore, where nothing was watching.

Fix. Writes to the same resource were serialised in the executor keyed by resource id, and the tool was changed to patch named fields rather than replace the record — which removed the read-modify-write entirely and made the parallelism safe again. The general lesson is that parallel calls are not parallel effects, and the model has no way to tell the difference.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Parallel Tool Calling & Tool Batching — the mechanism.

  • concurrency and parallelism — concurrency across the run.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §4 Read tools vs write tools — direction is exactly the eligibility axis here.

  • §9 Latency — this is the single biggest lever in that section.

  • §5 Shared state across agents — the same race one layer up.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — parallel retrieval is where the latency budget is won.

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — serialising the write path is what keeps it correct.

notes.title: Adopt MCP, and build a server or consume one
notes.category: Agentic System Design (§4 Tool Layer Design)

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The protocol, its primitives and its host/client/server model — Model Context Protocol: specification

  • Transports and connection lifecycle, which decide your deployment shape — MCP: transports

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) — what MCP is and how it's structured.

  • Building vs Consuming MCP Servers — the two sides of the protocol.

  • Why MCP Matters for Architects — the integration argument.

What this note adds: whether it's worth the indirection for your system. MCP's value is M + N integrations instead of M × N, which is a real win for a platform and overhead for a single agent with four in-house tools.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What MCP buys? M + N integrations instead of M × N — tools decoupled from agents.
When it's overhead? One agent, a handful of in-house tools, no reuse.
The deployment consequence? Transport choice — local stdio versus a remote server you now operate.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

MCP earns its place when tools need to be reused across agents or consumed from third parties, because it turns M × N bespoke integrations into M + N protocol implementations. For a single agent with four tools I wrote myself, it's a layer of indirection buying nothing. So my split is: consume MCP servers when a vendor provides one — that's free integration — and build one only when a capability of mine has more than one consumer. The consequence people underestimate is deployment: a remote MCP server is a service you now run, authenticate and scale.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Direct function tools One agent, in-house capabilities, no reuse. No interop — another agent reimplements them. Four tools, one codebase, one team.
Consume MCP servers A vendor or internal team already exposes one. A dependency on their schema and availability. The integration exists; you'd otherwise write a client.
Build an MCP server Your capability has several consumers, or partners need it. A service to run, authenticate, version and scale. Two agents have already implemented the same tool.
MCP gateway Many servers and many agents inside one organisation. Platform work: registry, auth brokering, policy. You can't say who is allowed to call what.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Direct tools Nothing — functions behind your tool layer. Lowest overhead. You own everything; nothing to integrate.
Consume An MCP client plus transport config per server. Network hop per call on remote transports. Their outage is your outage; version drift is your problem.
Build A server implementing the protocol, with its own auth. A service to run, plus per-call overhead. Consumers you don't control depend on your schema — versioning matters.
Gateway A broker between agents and servers, holding policy and credentials. Another hop; a component that must not go down. Central place for allowlisting, audit and credential exchange.

The redraw test: consuming or building moves tools out of your process and onto the network, so the diagram gains a boundary — with the auth and failure handling that implies.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We adopted MCP across the board and our simplest agent got slower and harder to debug."

Root cause. A team standardised on MCP for every tool, including four in-house functions used by exactly one agent. Those became a local server over stdio, which meant process management, a serialisation boundary, and stack traces that stopped at the protocol edge. Nothing was reused — there was only one consumer — so the M + N benefit never materialised, while the indirection cost was paid on every call and every debugging session.

Fix. In-house single-consumer tools went back to direct function calls, and MCP was kept for the two third-party servers where it was doing real work. The rule they adopted afterwards is the useful output: adopt the protocol at the point where a second consumer appears, not before.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • MCP Transports & Connection Lifecycle — the deployment consequence.

  • A2A & Agent Interoperability — the agent-to-agent sibling protocol.

  • OpenAPI & Tool-Spec Standards — the OpenAPI-to-tools path, and its granularity trap.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §4 Tool granularity — an MCP server's schema is a public contract, so granularity gets harder to change.

  • §2 Where authority to act lives — a remote server means the boundary is crossed over a network.

  • §11 Least privilege — credential exchange to a server you don't run is the confused-deputy case.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Internal agent platform — the gateway row is that problem's core integration decision.

  • §14 Browser / computer-use agent — usually consumed as a server rather than built.

notes.title: Give the agent a shell, or keep the action space typed
notes.category: Agentic System Design (§4 Tool Layer Design)

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Code execution as the action space, and why the sandbox is mandatory — CodeAct: executable code actions elicit better LLM agents (arXiv 2402.01030)

  • Computer use — the capability and its stated operational risks — Anthropic: computer use

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • CodeAct — code as the action representation.

  • Computer Use or Browser Use — browser and desktop control.

  • sandboxing and isolation — how the sandbox is built.

What this note adds: what you're actually trading. Both options buy an unbounded action space by giving up the typed contract that every other tool decision in this section depends on — so the boundary moves from the schema to the sandbox, and everything upstream changes.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What you gain? An unbounded action space — composition the tool list never anticipated.
What you give up? The typed contract. Validation moves from schema to sandbox.
The non-negotiable? Isolation: container or microVM, allowlisted egress, no ambient credentials.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Code execution gives the agent an action space I can't enumerate, which is exactly what makes it powerful and exactly what I lose. Every other decision in the tool layer assumes a typed contract I can validate; a shell has none, so the enforcement point moves from the schema to the sandbox — isolation, allowlisted egress, no ambient credentials, and a time limit. I reach for it when the task genuinely needs composition I can't anticipate, like data analysis. Computer and browser use is the same trade with worse reliability, since it's also subject to UIs changing underneath you.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Typed tools only The action space is enumerable. The default. The agent can't compose anything you didn't provide. You can list the operations the task needs.
Code execution, sandboxed Analysis, transformation, composition you can't enumerate. A sandbox to run and secure; no schema to validate against. "Compute whatever this question needs from this data."
Browser / computer use The only interface to the system is a UI. Flaky, slow, and breaks when the UI changes. A legacy system with no API.
Code generation without execution You want the artifact, not the effect. A human or a pipeline must run it — that's the safety. The deliverable is a script someone reviews.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Typed tools Schema validation at the boundary. Predictable per call. Rejections are typed and diagnosable.
Code execution A sandbox: container or microVM, egress allowlist, filesystem and time limits. Compute per run, plus sandbox startup. Sandbox escapes are the risk; image and dependency hygiene is ongoing.
Browser use Sandbox plus a driver; screenshots or accessibility tree into the model. Many slow steps; vision tokens are expensive. Flakiness dominates. UI changes are unannounced breakage.
Generate, don't run An artifact store and a review step. Cheapest of the three. Review becomes the bottleneck — and the control.

The redraw test: code execution replaces the validation box with a sandbox box. If your diagram has neither, the agent is running model-authored code on your infrastructure with nothing between.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The analysis agent exfiltrated data from a notebook, and the audit couldn't say what it sent."

Root cause. The sandbox was a container with resource limits and no network policy, because the threat model had been about runaway compute rather than about egress. The agent's task involved reading a dataset and producing summary statistics, and a prompt-injected instruction inside one of the input files convinced it to POST the contents to an external endpoint. The container had general internet access, and outbound calls made from inside it weren't part of the agent's tool trace, so the audit log showed a successful code execution with no record of what left.

Fix. Egress allowlisting at the sandbox boundary, credentials removed from the execution environment and passed only as narrowly scoped values, and network activity logged as part of the run trace. The generalisable lesson is that a sandbox sized for resource isolation is not sized for data isolation, and code execution combines a broad read with an outbound path — which is the exfiltration shape.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • sandboxing and isolation — the boundary this decision relies on.

  • CodeAct — code as the action space.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §4 Validate at the boundary — code execution is the case where schema validation cannot apply.

  • §11 Sandboxing — this decision is what makes that section mandatory rather than optional.

  • §11 The lethal trifecta — private data plus untrusted content plus an egress path, all in one tool.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Coding agent — the sandbox is the whole operational story.

  • §14 Data / SQL analyst agent — where code execution is genuinely the right action space.

  • §14 Browser / computer-use agent — flakiness and action space are the design's core tension.

notes.title: Escalation as a callable tool, or as a terminal state
notes.category: Agentic System Design (§4 Tool Layer Design)

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Human intervention as a designed trigger rather than an error path — A practical guide to building agents (OpenAI, PDF)

  • Interrupts that pause a run and resume it with a payload — LangGraph: durable execution

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Human-as-a-tool — the pattern of exposing a person as a callable action.

  • human-in-the-loop — approval gates and where they sit.

What this note adds: the fork between asking a human mid-run and handing off at the end. The first needs durability and a typed payload; the second doesn't. Choosing the first without the durability is where runs get stuck.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Tool or terminal state? Tool if the run continues after the answer; terminal if it doesn't.
What a human tool needs? A typed payload, a durable pause, a timeout, and a default on expiry.
The failure without a default? Silently stuck runs nobody is counting.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

If the agent needs an answer to keep working — a missing parameter, a judgement call, an approval — then the human is a tool: it's called mid-run, the run pauses durably, and the answer comes back as a typed payload. If the agent is done and a person takes over, that's a terminal state and a handoff, which is much simpler and needs none of the machinery. Teams get into trouble by building the first without the durability, so the run holds state in memory and quietly dies when the worker restarts before anyone replies.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Human as a tool The run continues once the human answers. Durable pause, a queue with an SLA, timeouts and defaults. "Ask the user which account they meant, then carry on."
Terminal escalation The agent is finished and a person takes over. Nothing structural — it's an exit path. Confidence too low to proceed at all.
Approval gate The action is decided; a human authorises it. Same durability as a tool, plus an explicit deny path. Irreversible or high-value writes.
Async notify, keep going A human should know but needn't respond. Nothing blocks — but nobody is accountable either. Audit or awareness rather than a decision.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Human as a tool Durable checkpoint, a task queue, a resume-with-payload path. Wall-clock unbounded; token cost pauses with the run. Queue age and SLA become live metrics; stuck runs need an alarm.
Terminal escalation An exit path and a handoff format. The run ends — cost stops. Escalation rate is the headline metric.
Approval gate All of the above plus an explicit denial branch. Same as the tool. Approval latency joins p95; expiry needs a default.
Async notify A notification sink. Negligible. Nobody is accountable — easy to over-use until it's noise.

The redraw test: human-as-a-tool puts a pause and a queue in the diagram and makes the checkpointer mandatory. Terminal escalation is an arrow leaving the flow. Those are very different pictures for what sounds like the same feature.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "About one in thirty runs just never finishes. No error, no timeout, nothing in the logs."

Root cause. The agent could ask a human for clarification mid-run, implemented as a blocking wait on an in-memory future while the worker held the run state. Most clarifications came back within minutes and it worked. When a request arrived near a deploy, or the user didn't reply before the pod recycled, the state vanished — the run was neither completed nor failed, so nothing counted it and no alert fired. The requests kept appearing in the human queue, and answering them did nothing.

Fix. The pause became a durable checkpoint with the run id in the queued task, so answering resumes from state rather than signalling a live process. Every request also got a timeout with a default — proceed with the safe assumption, or escalate to terminal — so a run could no longer sit in limbo. The lesson is that a human tool is an unbounded wait by definition, and any unbounded wait held in memory is a run you will eventually lose.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Human-as-a-tool — the pattern itself.

  • human-in-the-loop — approval gates, the adjacent case.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §1 Autonomy level — supervised autonomy is implemented as this tool.

  • §7 HITL as a durable pause — choosing the tool form makes durability mandatory.

  • §2 Sync vs async runs — a human tool forces the async side of that fork regardless of run length.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — approval on refunds is exactly this.

  • §14 Back-office workflow automation — HITL checkpoints are the design's spine.
